Australians vote directly for the Prime Minister.
Voters elect their local member. The Prime Minister is the leader of the party or coalition that has the support of most members in the House of Representatives.
Voting in federal elections is optional once you turn 18.
Enrolling and voting are compulsory for eligible citizens aged 18 and over. Not voting without a valid reason brings a fine.
The Governor-General is elected by the Australian people.
The Governor-General is appointed by the King on the advice of the Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister can sack a judge whose decisions the government dislikes.
Federal judges can only be removed by both houses of Parliament for proved misbehaviour or incapacity. That protects the independence of the courts.
A referendum passes if more than half of all Australian voters say Yes.
It needs a double majority: a national majority of voters and a majority of voters in at least four of the six states.
Local councils can make any law they like for their area.
Councils only have the powers their state government gives them. States create councils and can dismiss one that is failing.
Australia has two levels of government, federal and state.
There are three. Local councils are the third level, even though the Constitution does not mention them.
Parliament can change the Australian Constitution by passing a law.
Only the people can change it, at a referendum. Parliament proposes the change; voters decide.
A person accused of a crime has to prove they are innocent.
The prosecution must prove guilt. Everyone is presumed innocent until proven guilty.
Judges in Australia are elected.
Judges are appointed by the executive government, not elected. That is one reason they are not swayed by popularity.
If you believe a law is unfair, you are allowed to break it.
The rule of law means every person must follow the law. You can campaign to change a law, but not ignore it.
Only people born in Australia can be Australian citizens.
People become citizens by birth, by descent from an Australian parent, or by applying after migrating here.
A party needs more than half of all votes in Australia to form government.
Government is formed by winning seats, not the national vote. A party or coalition needs at least 76 of the 150 seats in the House of Representatives.
Independents cannot be elected because they do not belong to a party.
Anyone eligible can stand. Several independents sit in the current federal Parliament.
The Opposition has no job to do until the next election.
The Opposition questions ministers, scrutinises bills and offers an alternative government. That is part of keeping government accountable.
Australia became a nation on 26 January 1788.
Federation was 1 January 1901, when the six colonies joined under the Constitution. 1788 was the arrival of the First Fleet at Sydney Cove.
You have to be 21 to vote in Australia.
The voting age has been 18 since 1973. You can enrol at 16 or 17 so you are ready.
A Member of Parliament only has to listen to people who voted for them.
An MP represents everyone in their electorate, whoever they voted for. Anyone can contact them.
Freedom of speech means you can say anything without legal consequences.
Australians can criticise the government freely, but laws still cover threats, defamation and racial vilification.
Equity means treating everyone exactly the same.
That is equality. Equity gives people different help depending on what they need, so everyone gets a fair chance to take part.
The Prime Minister is described in the Australian Constitution.
The Constitution never mentions the Prime Minister. The role comes from tradition and convention.
Once Parliament passes a law, it can never be changed.
Parliament can amend or repeal any law it has made. Laws change as society changes.
Police decide whether a person is guilty.
Police investigate and charge. Courts decide guilt. That is the separation of powers at work.
The King personally approves every Australian law.
Royal assent is given by the Governor-General, or a state Governor, and it is a formality once Parliament has passed the bill.
The 1967 referendum gave Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people the right to vote.
The right to enrol and vote federally came in 1962. The 1967 referendum changed how First Nations people were counted and let the federal Parliament make laws for them.
Only citizens can take part in civic action like petitions or community meetings.
Anyone can sign a petition, attend a meeting or contact an MP. Voting is the one that is reserved for citizens.
Local councils collect income tax.
Councils raise money mainly from rates on property, plus fees and grants. Income tax is collected by the federal government.
Everyone in Australia gets a free lawyer for any court case.
Legal aid is available for some people and some cases, mostly based on income and the seriousness of the matter. Access to justice is still a work in progress.
Being popular with everyone is one of the five characteristics of an effective law.
The five are: reflects society's values, enforceable, known, clear and understood, and stable. No law is popular with everyone.
The Australian Constitution came into effect on 1 January 1901.
That is Federation, when six separate colonies became one nation with one federal Parliament.
Only 8 of the 45 proposed changes to the Constitution have ever been approved.
The double majority is hard to achieve. The most recent referendum, in 2023, was the 45th proposal.
The 1967 referendum recorded the highest Yes vote in Australian history, over 90 per cent.
Nearly 91 per cent of voters said Yes, and it passed in every state.
A party or coalition needs at least 76 of the 150 seats to govern in its own right.
76 is the first number past half. A party with 75 would need support from the crossbench.
If a state law and a federal law clash in an area both can make laws about, the federal law wins.
Section 109 of the Constitution says so. The state law is invalid to the extent of the clash.
First Nations peoples have lived on and cared for Country for at least 65,000 years.
Archaeological evidence from sites such as Madjedbebe in the Northern Territory supports this.
Australians aged 18 and over can be called to serve on a jury.
Juries are drawn from the electoral roll. Serving if selected is a responsibility of citizenship.
Victoria was the first place in the world to make wearing seatbelts compulsory.
The law came in in 1970 and road deaths fell. Other states and countries copied it.
You can be an Australian citizen and a citizen of another country at the same time.
Dual citizenship has been allowed since 2002. Many Australians hold two passports.
Federal elections for the House of Representatives must be held at least every three years.
Three years is the maximum term. A government can call an election earlier.
The Australian Electoral Commission runs federal elections and is independent of the government of the day.
Independence matters so that the people in power cannot run the election in their own favour.
The High Court can declare a law invalid if it goes against the Constitution.
That is the judiciary checking the legislature, part of the separation of powers.
Anyone can sit in the public gallery at Parliament House and watch a debate.
Parliament is open to the public, including Question Time, when ministers must answer questions about their decisions.
Most Australians are represented by three levels of government at once.
You live in a federal electorate, a state electorate and, almost everywhere, a local council area.
Local councils are not mentioned in the Australian Constitution.
Councils exist under state laws. Proposals to add them to the Constitution failed at referendums in 1974 and 1988.
A bill must pass both houses of federal Parliament before it can become law.
After the House of Representatives and the Senate agree, the Governor-General gives royal assent.
A government with fewer than half the seats can still govern.
A minority government relies on crossbench members agreeing to support it on key votes.
In a House of Representatives election you number every box on the ballot paper.
This is preferential voting. If your first choice is knocked out, your vote moves to your next preference.
Australia is both a democracy and a monarchy.
It is a constitutional monarchy: the King is head of state, but the people elect the Parliament that governs.
Courts are usually open to the public.
Open justice lets people see that trials are fair. There are exceptions, such as cases involving children.
A judge must step aside from a case involving a relative.
A judge with a personal connection cannot be seen as impartial, so another judge hears the case. This protects fairness.
A law can be fair and clear but still fail if people do not know it exists.
Being known is one of the five characteristics of an effective law. Nobody can follow a rule they have never heard of.
Ministers must answer questions from other MPs in Parliament every sitting day.
Question Time is one way Parliament holds the government accountable for its decisions.
